html:
The cult of the god Mithras, a Roman mystery religion that spread across the empire from the late 1st century CE and lasted until the late 4th century.

The name comes from Mithra, a god of the Iranian and Zoroastrian world, but how much the Roman cult owed to Persia is debated. It may have been largely a new creation. Its members left almost no writings, so it is known mainly from its temples and images.

  • Members, all men, met in small, dark, cave-like temples called mithraea, eating a shared meal on benches along the walls.
  • The central image shows Mithras killing a bull, with a dog, a snake and a scorpion.
  • Members rose through seven grades, from Raven to Father.

It was popular with soldiers, traders and imperial officials, so mithraea turn up along the frontiers, from the Rhine and Danube to Hadrian's Wall, and in port towns such as Ostia, which had many. One was found in London in 1954.

As Christianity became the religion of the emperors, the cult died out, and under Theodosius I pagan worship was banned.
sum: The cult of the god Mithras, a Roman mystery religion that spread across the empire from the late 1st century CE and lasted until the late 4th century.
